name: prokinetic and antidiarrheal drugs overview
title: Prokinetic and antidiarrheal drugs: speed a slow gut with a D2 antagonist (metoclopramide or domperidone), a 5-HT4 agonist (prucalopride) or erythromycin, never with bleeding, obstruction or perforation; slow or dry diarrhea with opioid agonists (loperamide, diphenoxylate, eluxadoline), bismuth subsalicylate or bile acid resins; each with when to choose it and what rules it out

root.title: Gut too SLOW, or too FAST? Which drug, and what rules it out?
lines: a prokinetic must COORDINATE motility: simply boosting acetylcholine only gives uncoordinated contraction
diarrhea: treat the CAUSE (pathogen, inflammation) and prevent DEHYDRATION first

groups.title: TOO SLOW: PROKINETICS
lines: gastroparesis, constipation, some nausea and vomiting
NEVER with a GI bleed, bowel obstruction or perforation

groups.title: TOO FAST: ANTIDIARRHEALS
lines: slow the gut, or cut secretion
irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) with diarrhea: alosetron, a 5-HT3 ANTAGONIST, slows it

head: h
Dopamine (D2) antagonists
metoclopramide, domperidone
use: • also a serotonin agonist: double effect
Domperidone: stays OUT of the brain
avoid: QT prolongation: care in heart disease

head: h
Erythromycin
a macrolide: motilin agonist
use: Revs up the migrating motor complex

head: h
Opioid agonists
↓ motility, secretion, absorption
use: • over the counter, little brain entry
avoid: NOT with past pancreatitis, alcoholism or no gallbladder

head: h
Bismuth subsalicylate
↑ fluid absorption, binds E. coli toxin
h
Bile acid-binding resins
cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam
use: • itch from biliary or liver disease
avoid: • give 1 h before or 4 h after them
